ready1_open_rewrite.title: SciVerse open question
ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: Behavioral endocrinologists captured male individuals of territorial birds during a year to measure their testosterone (T) levels. In this population, male individuals may play one of two roles: (1) remain in the natal group and help raise young brothers and sisters; (2) leave the natal group and establish a new territory. Based on the above information and the following two histograms, from an evolutionary perspective, what is the observed pattern of testosterone levels in this population most likely to be?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: the upper histogram is labeled “Non-breeding season”, and the vertical axis is average testosterone level. In the non-breeding season, the bars for helper male and breeding male are both very low, about 10. The lower histogram is labeled “Breeding season”, the average T level of helper male is still about 10, while the average T level of breeding male rises obviously, about 50. That is to say, in the breeding season only breeding males that establish or possess territories have significantly increased T levels, and helper males maintain low levels. Then reason: the question stem states that males have two roles: one remains in the natal group to help raise younger brothers and sisters, and the other leaves and establishes a new territory. Breeding males in the breeding season need to carry out territory defense, courtship, and mating competition, so higher T levels may increase their reproductive success; helper males do not directly compete for reproductive opportunities, and maintaining low T levels can reduce aggression and the physiological costs brought by hormones, and is beneficial for caring for relatives. Since this regulation of T levels changes with season and social role, and may increase individual or kin fitness, from an evolutionary perspective it is most likely an adaptation.
